title: Robust estimates
objectives: Use medians, trimmed means and robust regression when outliers dominate.

screens.title: One month moves the mean
screens.prose: A fund's nine monthly returns, in %. One month a single position paid off: 25%. Drag that month and watch three summaries of a typical month.

derive.caption: Mean {{fixed((5.5 + p.x)/9, 3)}}%, median {{fixed(min(max(p.x, 0.8), 0.9), 3)}}%, 20% trimmed mean {{fixed((5.5 + p.x - min(p.x, -0.5) - max(p.x, 1.5))/7, 3)}}%

screens.question: With the big month at 25%, what is the mean monthly return?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the eight other months, 5.5, to 25 and divide by 9.

byKey.eight: You averaged the other eight months only.

explain.text: At 25% the mean is 3.389% and follows the big month wherever you drag it. The median stays between 0.8 and 0.9. Set the month to 1.0 and the mean falls to 0.722%.

screens.title: How far can one month drag
screens.prose: Replace the 25% month by an ordinary 1.0%.

derive.caption: Mean {{fixed((5.5 + p.x)/9, 3)}}%, median {{fixed(min(max(p.x, 0.8), 0.9), 3)}}%, 20% trimmed mean {{fixed((5.5 + p.x - min(p.x, -0.5) - max(p.x, 1.5))/7, 3)}}%

screens.question: What is the mean now?

hints.text: The eight fixed months sum to 5.5.

feedback.correct: 0.722%: one month had moved the mean by 2.7 points.

byKey.med: That is the median, which did not move.

explain.text: The mean is now 0.722%. The **breakdown point** is the share of data that can be moved arbitrarily far before an estimate follows. The mean's is 0, as one month suffices; the median's is one half.

screens.title: Trim the ends
screens.prose: A 20% trimmed mean cuts 20% from each end before averaging: with $n = 9$, $\lfloor 0.2 \times 9 \rfloor = 1$ month from each end.
screens.question: What is the 20% trimmed mean of the nine months?

hints.text: Sort and drop the smallest and largest.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drop one month from each end, then average seven.

byKey.one: You dropped only the lowest month. Trim both ends.
byKey.nine: You divided the seven-month sum by 9.

explain.text: `scipy.stats.trim_mean(x, 0.2)` gives 0.857 too. Huber's M-estimate ($k = 1.345$, MAD scale), which shrinks rather than cuts, gives 0.93.

screens.title: A robust spread
screens.prose: The median absolute deviation (MAD) is the median of $|x_j - \text{median}|$. Scaled by 1.4826, it estimates $\sigma$ for normal data. The median is 0.9 and the sorted absolute deviations are 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3, 0.6, 1.1, 1.4, 24.1.
screens.question: What is the scaled MAD?

hints.text: The middle of the nine sorted deviations.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the middle deviation and scale it.

byKey.raw: That is the raw MAD. Scale by 1.4826 to compare with an SD.
byKey.sd: That is the ordinary SD, inflated by the one month.

explain.text: One month inflates the SD to 8.130% while the scaled MAD says 0.4448%. `median_abs_deviation(x, scale='normal')` agrees.

screens.title: Bootstrapping the mean
screens.prose: Bootstrap the mean as in `estimation` lesson 11: each run draws 9 months with replacement and averages them. Run 1,000 resamples.
screens.question: What is the chance that a resample holds no copy of the 25% month?

hints.text: Each draw misses the big month with probability 8/9.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise 8/9 to the ninth power.

byKey.one: That is the chance of exactly one copy.
byKey.ninth: That is one draw. A resample has nine.

explain.text: The histogram splits into clusters by the number of copies of 25: none (34.6%), one (39.0%), two (19.5%), three (5.7%). The bootstrap SD is about 2.555, faithfully reporting an unstable mean. A resample's median reaches 25 only with five or more copies of it, a 0.14% chance.

screens.title: A beta and one wild day
screens.prose: Sixty days of market and stock returns. On day 40 the market rose 0.85% but a takeover rumour sent the stock up 25%. OLS gives $\hat\beta = 1.584$; the true beta was 1.2. Tukey's bisquare fit (dashed) gives 1.143. Drag day 40.

derive.caption: Day 40 sits {{fixed((p39.y - 0.005175 - 1.142954*p39.x)/0.88977, 1)}} scale units above the bisquare line.

screens.question: Drag day 40 straight up to a stock return of 40%, keeping the market at 0.85%. What slope does the OLS fit show?

hints.text: Read the slope in the OLS label.

feedback.correct: 1.854: one day moves OLS from 1.278 (at 8%) to 1.854 (at 40%). The bisquare line stays put while day 40 stays an outlier.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Move day 40 to 40% and read the OLS slope.

byKey.start: That is the OLS slope with day 40 at 25%.
byKey.tukey: That is the bisquare slope, which ignores day 40 while it sits more than 4.17 bps off the line.

explain.text: OLS slopes 1.278 at 8%, 1.404 at 15% and 1.854 at 40%. The bisquare fit gives day 40 weight 0, so it drops out of the fitting equations. That holds while the caption shows day 40 more than 4.685 scale units from the line.

screens.title: Just delete it
screens.prose: A colleague says: "Day 40 is obviously an error. Delete it and run OLS." Without day 40, OLS gives $\hat\beta = 1.151$.

derive.caption: Day 40 sits {{fixed((p39.y - 0.005175 - 1.142954*p39.x)/0.88977, 1)}} scale units above the bisquare line.

screens.question: What is wrong with deleting the day by hand?

options.text: The rule "drop what looks odd" is chosen after seeing the result, and the day may be real
Nothing: 1.151 is close to the truth
options.why: It happens to work here. Next time the odd-looking day may be the one that matters.

options.text: Only that 59 days are too few
options.why: Sample size is not the issue; the choice made from the data is.
Day 40 has an ordinary market move; it is an outlier in $y$, not a leverage point.

hints.text: When was the rule "delete it" chosen?
A robust method states its rule in advance.

feedback.correct: A rule fixed after seeing the data is not a rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask when the deletion was decided.

byKey.ok: You judged by the answer. A rule must not depend on whether you like the result.

explain.text: A takeover rumour is a real day. The bisquare fit downweights extreme residuals by a stated rule, $c = 4.685$ scale units, fixed before the data were seen.

screens.title: The median of all slopes
screens.prose: Theil-Sen takes the slope through every pair of days and reports their median. Pairs with the same market return have no slope.

derive.caption: Day 40 sits {{fixed((p39.y - 0.005175 - 1.142954*p39.x)/0.88977, 1)}} scale units above the bisquare line.

screens.question: How many pairs of days are there among 60?

feedback.correct: 1,770 pairs; 6 share a market return, so 1,764 slopes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count unordered pairs.

byKey.used: That is the slopes that exist; the question asks for all pairs.

explain.text: The median of the 1,764 slopes is 1.2346, close to the true 1.2. One day can shift at most a few dozen slopes, so the median barely moves.

screens.title: Robust estimates in code
screens.prose: Write the scaled MAD, a trimmed mean, and the bisquare fit by IRLS. Start from OLS and set the scale to median$(|r|)/0.6745$, exactly `norm.ppf(0.75)`. Weight each day by $(1 - u^2)^2$ for $|u| = |r|/(cs) < 1$ and 0 beyond, then refit.

derive.caption: Day 40 sits {{fixed((p39.y - 0.005175 - 1.142954*p39.x)/0.88977, 1)}} scale units above the bisquare line.

Weighted solve: `np.linalg.solve(X.T @ (w[:, None] * X), X.T @ (w * y))`.

explain.text: The scale settles at 0.88977, so day 40's residual of about 24 is 27 scale units out. Its weight is exactly 0. The bisquare line is then OLS on the other days, reweighted.

screens.question: Complete `rlm_fits`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm


def rlm_fits(X, y):
    """Return (Tukey params, Huber params, Huber weight on day 40)."""
    ...
widget.solution:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm


def rlm_fits(X, y):
    t = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.TukeyBiweight()).fit(conv='coefs', tol=1e-13)
    h = sm.RLM(y, X, M=sm.robust.norms.HuberT()).fit(conv='coefs', tol=1e-13)
    return t.params, h.params, h.weights[39]

screens.title: Sizing a hedge
screens.prose: A desk holds £5m of the stock and hedges its market exposure by selling the index: beta times £5m. OLS says 1.583828, the bisquare fit 1.142954.

derive.caption: Day 40 sits {{fixed((p39.y - 0.005175 - 1.142954*p39.x)/0.88977, 1)}} scale units above the bisquare line.

screens.question: How much more index, in pounds, does the OLS hedge sell than the bisquare hedge?

feedback.correct: £2.2m of extra index: the OLS hedge is about a third too big against the true beta of 1.2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the difference in betas by £5m.

byKey.ols: That is the whole OLS hedge.
byKey.rob: That is the whole bisquare hedge.

explain.text: OLS would sell £7.92m of index, the bisquare £5.71m: £2,204,370 more. Against a true beta of 1.2, OLS over-hedges by about a third, so a robust fit is the desk's default.

ideas: One month moves the mean (breakdown point 0) but not the median (one half): 3.389% against 0.9%.
Trimmed means, the scaled MAD and M-estimates give typical values and spreads that one wild day cannot drag.
Robust regression: the bisquare fit gives a takeover day weight 0, a beta of 1.143 against OLS's 1.584.
summary.trap: Deleting an outlier by hand after seeing the fit: state a robust rule in advance instead.

quiz.prose: Of 20 daily returns, 11 are replaced by arbitrary garbage values.
quiz.question: Which estimate can still be trusted?

options.text: None of the usual ones: past half the data, even the median breaks down

options.why: The median's breakdown point is one half; with 11 of 20 corrupted it can be anywhere.
It cuts 4 from each end; 11 bad values cannot all be trimmed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 11 of 20 with each breakdown point.

explain.text: Breakdown points cap at one half: with most of the data corrupt, the corruption is the data.

quiz.prose: On one day the market fell 6% and the stock 12%. Both are far beyond every other day, but in line with a beta of 2.
quiz.question: Why can this day pull OLS without looking odd in the residuals?

options.text: It is a leverage point: its extreme $x$ lets it drag the line towards itself

options.why: Its $x$ is far from the rest, which gives it outsized influence on the slope.

options.text: It cannot pull OLS: its residual is small
options.why: Its residual is small because the line has moved to it.

feedback.correct: High leverage hides in small residuals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about how far its $x$ is from the others.

explain.text: A point far out in $x$ pulls the line towards itself, so its own residual looks ordinary. Check leverage as well as residuals.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Median of the absolute deviations from the median.

byKey.mean: That is the mean absolute deviation.

explain.text: Median 0.5; absolute deviations 0.4, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2, 8.5; their median is 0.2.
